# Objective

The `dosefitr` package provides tools for analysing dose-response curves and the subsequent calculation of GR, NDR and LGR metrics. This vignette walks through the main functionality of this using an example dataset included with the package.

First, load the package.

```{r echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dosefitr)
```

# Dose-response analysis

The `conc_data` dataset contains spheroid area measurements over time across a
range of drug concentrations. As before, we start by plotting the raw data.

```{r}
data("conc_data", package = "dosefitr")

ggplot2::ggplot(
  conc_data,
  ggplot2::aes(hours_from, area, colour = as.factor(concentration))
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::labs(colour = "log[M]")
```

`fit_concentrations()` fits a curve to each concentration. By default it tries
every model in `dosefitr_models` and selects the best fit, but this can be
restricted to a subset. For example, to consider only sigmoid models:

```{r}
conc_model <- fit_concentrations(
  data = conc_data,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area",
  treatment_column = "treatment_name",
  negative_control_name = "vehicle",
  concentration_column = "concentration",
  outlier_options = list(huber = TRUE, rout = TRUE),
  models = c("four_param_sigmoid", "five_param_sigmoid")
)

conc_model$plot
```

Or to consider all models except `beta_growth_decay`:

```{r}
conc_model <- fit_concentrations(
  data = conc_data,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area",
  treatment_column = "treatment_name",
  negative_control_name = "vehicle",
  concentration_column = "concentration",
  outlier_options = list(huber = TRUE, rout = TRUE),
  models = setdiff(names(dosefitr_models), "beta_growth_decay")
)

conc_model$plot
```

## Identifying complete killing

The two highest concentrations (-4 and -4.5 log M) clearly break from the trend
of the rest of the series. At these doses the spheres were completely killed,
so the measured areas are not real signal; they are segmentation artefacts from
debris and dead-cell material rather than intact spheres.

This kind of non-monotonic response can be flagged automatically. Setting
`monotonic_check = TRUE` warns when the response reverses direction at high
concentrations, which is a useful prompt to go back and check the images.

```{r}
conc_model <- fit_concentrations(
  data = conc_data,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area",
  treatment_column = "treatment_name",
  negative_control_name = "vehicle",
  concentration_column = "concentration",
  outlier_options = list(huber = TRUE, rout = TRUE),
  models = setdiff(names(dosefitr_models), "beta_growth_decay"),
  monotonic_check = TRUE
)
```

Where you know a concentration caused complete killing, add a logical `exclude`
column to the data. Wells marked `TRUE` are treated as 100% killing rather than
fitted from their (artefactual) measured areas. If you would rather drop these
concentrations from the analysis entirely, filter them out of the data instead.

```{r}
conc_data <- dplyr::mutate(
  conc_data,
  exclude = concentration %in% c(-4, -4.5)
)

conc_model <- fit_concentrations(
  data = conc_data,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area",
  treatment_column = "treatment_name",
  negative_control_name = "vehicle",
  concentration_column = "concentration",
  outlier_options = list(huber = TRUE, rout = TRUE),
  models = setdiff(names(dosefitr_models), "beta_growth_decay"),
  monotonic_check = TRUE
)
```

## Visualising the results

Area over time, coloured by concentration. Concentrations marked as complete
killing are shown in red.

```{r}
plot_curve_concentration(
  model_list = conc_model$model_list,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  y_var = "area",
  treatment_column = "treatment_name",
  concentration_column = "concentration",
  negative_control_name = "vehicle"
)
```

Growth rate (GR) over time at each concentration shows how the drug alters the
rate of growth throughout the experiment.

```{r}
plot_metric_time <- plot_curve_concentration_metric_time(
  model_list = conc_model$model_list,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  metric = "gr",
  treatment_column = "treatment_name",
  concentration_column = "concentration",
  negative_control_name = "vehicle"
)

plot_metric_time$plot
```

Finally, the dose-response curve summarises growth inhibition as a function of
drug concentration, incorporating GR values measured at all timepoints across the experiment.

```{r}
plot_metric_dose <- plot_curve_concentration_metric_dose(
  model_list = conc_model$model_list,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  metric = "gr",
  treatment_column = "treatment_name",
  concentration_column = "concentration",
  negative_control_name = "vehicle"
)

plot_metric_dose$plot
```

We can also use the LGR score to visualise response. See the `dosefitr` manuscript on a full explanation of this metric and it's interpretation.

```{r}
plot_lgr_score(
  model_list = conc_model$model_list,
  x_var = "hours_from",
  metric = "gr",
  treatment_column = "treatment_name",
  concentration_column = "concentration",
  negative_control_name = "vehicle"
)
```
